name: Wigmore diet

lead: The Wigmore diet centres on uncooked plant foods, sprouts, fermented foods and wheatgrass juice. Proponents say it detoxifies the body and, through a clean, nutrient-dense intake, supports clearer skin, energy and a leaner look.

It was developed by Lithuanian-American health advocate Ann Wigmore (1909-1994) and spread through the Hippocrates Health Institute and her books. Critics including consumer-health groups dispute the detox rationale.

paras: Followers eat raw vegetables, sprouts, seeds and fermented foods and drink wheatgrass juice, often as part of a stay at a wellness institute.

Massachusetts regulators took legal action against Wigmore in the 1980s over claims about treating diabetes, cancer and AIDS. Critics say the diet may be restrictive and that its detox claims are unsupported; people with medical conditions are generally advised to keep standard care.

chain: Replace cooked and processed foods with raw plants and wheatgrass
Claimed detoxification and higher nutrient intake
Claimed clearer skin and leaner body
angle.text: Followers describe the diet as a way to get clearer skin and a lighter physique through a plant-based raw intake. These effects are claims of practitioners, and no controlled trial of the regimen is cited here.

lead: The Wigmore diet is a raw-food regimen built around wheatgrass juice, sprouts and uncooked vegetables, named for Ann Wigmore (1909-1994), a Lithuanian-American advocate of raw foods [1]. Proponents present it as a way to cleanse the body and improve general health, which followers extend to clearer skin and vitality.
Wigmore drew on the earlier raw-food sanatorium of Maximilian Bircher-Benner (opened near Zurich in 1904) and from the 1940s promoted wheatgrass and raw foods, arguing that cooking weakened food [1].
Her Boston group became the Hippocrates Health Institute in 1982; in 1987 Brian Clement moved it to West Palm Beach, Florida [1].

paras: Wigmore was born in Lithuania, became a US citizen in 1942 and wrote roughly 25 books [1]. The Ann Wigmore Foundation received IRS nonprofit status in 1970, and an Ann Wigmore Natural Health Institute was founded in Puerto Rico [1].
Wigmore held that plants carried more concentrated life energy than meat and that wheatgrass and raw foods helped the body detoxify [1].

In 1982 the Massachusetts attorney general sued over claims that her program could reduce diabetics' insulin needs and replace childhood vaccination; in 1988 a suit over AIDS-cure pamphlets ended with a judge protecting her views under the First Amendment but ordering her to stop presenting herself as a physician [1]. Critics such as the National Council Against Health Fraud said the idea that chlorophyll detoxifies the body is erroneous [1].

timeline.event: Bircher-Benner opens a raw-food sanatorium near Zurich [1]
Wigmore's group renamed Hippocrates Health Institute; attorney general suit [1]
Institute moved to Florida under Brian Clement [1]
Wigmore dies in a fire in Boston [1]
